comments.author: @apreyenimarlinafitriyani5636
comments.text:
Indonesia is not just a country on a map. Indonesia is an idea.

Historically, Indonesia emerged from the struggles of people from different ethnic groups, languages, religions, and cultures who chose to build one nation rather than remain divided by their differences.

Ideologically, Indonesia is founded on Pancasila: belief in God, humanity, national unity, deliberative democracy, and social justice.

As a nation, being Indonesian does not mean sharing the same culture. It means learning to live together, respecting one another, and recognizing that our differences do not have to make us enemies.

The national character we should strive for is the courage to stand for what is right, care for others, work together, and demand justice for everyone—not just those in power.

Of course, Indonesia still faces serious problems. Corruption, inequality, environmental destruction, and poor public policies must be challenged and addressed.

But criticizing Indonesia's failures does not mean we should lose sight of what Indonesia is meant to stand for.

A nation is not defined only by how well its territory is designed. It is also defined by the values its people stand for and the systems they build together.

Indonesia is an unfinished ideal.

The question is not just whether Indonesia is well designed, but whether we are still willing to fight for the idea of an Indonesia that is just, united, and worthy of all its people.

replies.author: @pineapplesareyummy6352
replies.text: I think you missed India as a superpower. It has better geography, a larger territory and larger population. As for Indonesia, yes, it has a large landmass and population and has potential to be powerful. However, the geography works against it. Indonesia has 17,000 islands, and it (along with Philippines) just have to live with the fact an archipelago nation is difficult to develop. It is costly to move stuff around. A country like China can build a contiguous national railway, a contiguous national electricity grid. But this is impossible due to Indonesia's geography, and that's a major disadvantage until technology allows moving across water to be as easy & economical as moving across land. But that doesn't seem likely.
